query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase fcc high‐entropy alloys, rapid nanosegregation of principal elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, and Mn) to grain boundaries diminishes intergranular cohesion, thereby governing toughness loss through promoting intergranular crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, coarse-grained fcc high‐entropy alloy with a nominally homogeneous composition prior to segregation events.
generation.intervention: Implement a segregation-engineering heat treatment or add secondary phase formers (such as Cr-rich constituents) to modify grain boundary chemistry and suppress harmful nanosegregation.
generation.conditions: Quasi-static tensile deformation at room to moderately elevated temperatures where intergranular fracture is observed.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemical composition at grain boundaries—including the extent and pattern of nanosegregation of primary elements—and the presence or absence of stabilizing secondary phases.
generation.mechanism: Rapid nanosegregation of elements like Ni, Cr, and Mn to the grain boundaries reduces cohesive strength, making them more susceptible to crack initiation and intergranular fracture, which leads to a loss in toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples that receive segregation-engineering treatments to either shift segregation into benign secondary phases or achieve a more uniform grain boundary composition will exhibit improved ductility and higher fracture toughness compared to untreated alloys.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEAs that display marked ductility loss and intergranular cracking due to unsuppressed, deleterious nanosegregation at the grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: This mechanism primarily applies to multi-principal element, single-phase fcc HEAs under low-to-moderate temperature deformation; behavior may differ in alloys with different crystal structures or under extreme temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: Although nanosegregation is implicated in grain boundary decohesion, the precise kinetics and interplay between various segregating species remain to be fully quantified across different alloy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of HEA samples: one under standard conditions and another with a targeted segregation-engineering treatment (e.g., heat treatment promoting Cr-rich secondary phase formation at grain boundaries). Conduct tensile tests while using atom probe tomography or STEM-EDS to assess grain boundary compositions.
measurements: Grain boundary composition and segregation profiles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the segregation-engineered samples do not exhibit significant improvements in toughness and show similar grain boundary chemistry as the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

We revealed the key mechanism responsible for the loss of the ductility with increasing temperature, a phenomenon widely reported in the single-phase fcc HEAs that are composed of three or more elements of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni. SEM of tensioned sample surfaces of single-phase coarse-grained Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size around 50 μm) suggested that ductility loss is correlated with the intergranular cracking. However, TEM along GBs confirmed that there are no precipitates of secondary phases along GBs. On the basis of APT analysis, we explored that ductility loss is attributed to fast nanosegregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn separately into GBs, which reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to evade ductility loss by migrating fast segregation of the principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases in an example HEA, i.e., Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14. Our work not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a GB segregation engineering strategy of tailoring strength-ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.
